rv.q: Tom Hollander’s Berezovsky is a genie just let out of a bottle: squirming, stretching, roaring, carrying on multiple conversations.
Rupert Goold’s production proves as excitingly intelligent as it is refreshingly pacey over its two and a half hours.
This is a minor quibble in a sharp, taut, political drama that enriches the West End.
It’s great to see it in the West End: a play of real political heft about a crisis that concerns us all.

Tom Hollander returns in this icily sobering account of Putin’s rise to power … The star reprises his role as Boris Berezovsky, the 'kingmaker' who was instrumental in Putin's ascent and lived to regret it … So this depiction of Putin’s preventable progress to the heart of power makes for an icily sobering evening.
Morgan’s is far more reserved, as if it can never quite escape its British formality.
Yes, Peter Morgan’s excellent play is instructive and thoroughly absorbing.
The contrast in physical energy between the men is enthralling.
Keen gains a pugnacious stillness, like a compressed spring that could explode at any moment.

Oddly, despite a smattering of celebrity faces secreted about the stalls on opening night, the production seemed to have lost a little of the zing which characterised the play’s initial run at the more intimate Almeida venue in Islington.
Regardless, it’s riveting from start to finish.

This West End transfer of Peter Morgan’s award-winning play, Patriots, is rich in debate, in images and in a distinct sense that there must be so much more to say, and know, about a country whose current war with Ukraine has made it so relevant to us all.
Perhaps it’s Morgan’s writing, which feels authentic and truthful but tries to obligingly fit in too many details.

cn.t: Patriots earns strong reviews for its chilling, prescient portrait of Putin's rise, with Tom Hollander's barnstorming performance as oligarch Berezovsky widely praised. A few critics find it uneven, but most hail it as urgent, thrilling political drama.
